endorsements.title: 45 CFR 92.210, nondiscrimination in the use of patient care decision support tools
endorsements.issuer: US Department of Health and Human Services
endorsements.quote: A covered entity has an ongoing duty to make reasonable efforts to identify uses of patient care decision support tools in its health programs or activities that employ input variables or factors that measure race, color, national origin, sex, age, or disability.

endorsements.title: Utah HB 452 (2025), mental health chatbots
endorsements.quote: (xiv) implements measures to prevent discriminatory treatment of users; and

endorsements.title: Principles for augmented intelligence development, deployment, and use
endorsements.quote: The final rule prohibits discrimination by clinical algorithms and requires physicians, hospitals, health systems, and others to use “reasonable efforts” to both identify algorithmic discrimination and to mitigate resulting harms.

endorsements.title: Responsible Use of AI in Healthcare (RUAIH) guidance
endorsements.issuer: The Joint Commission and Coalition for Health AI
endorsements.quote: Regularly monitor and audit AI tools to identify and mitigate or manage biases when appropriate.

endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: The framework requires identifying and mitigating biases within training data to prevent unequal treatment and ensure consistent outcomes across all patient groups.

endorsements.title: Developing, purchasing, implementing and monitoring AI tools in radiology: practical considerations. A multi-society statement
endorsements.issuer: ACR, CAR, ESR, RANZCR, RSNA; Radiol Artif Intell 2024 (PMID 38251899, doi:10.1148/ryai.230513)
endorsements.quote: There is no easy or straightforward process for comprehensively identifying these biases, but it is incumbent upon us as physicians and data scientists to think about, search for and mitigate these biases; if these questions are unasked, they will most certainly remain unanswered.

commentary.bottom_line: No supplied study tests whether inventorying decision support tools that use protected-characteristic inputs, followed by efforts to find and reduce discrimination, changes outcomes for patients. The practice rests on a federal regulation (45 CFR 92.210), a Utah statute, and four professional guidance documents or frameworks, so covered entities face a legal duty that the evidence base does not yet inform.

perspectives.view: The evidence map contains zero studies that test the practice and zero studies that document the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated when no study addresses the question. The six endorsements reflect expert and regulatory consensus, and consensus does not substitute for measured effects on detection of bias or on patient outcomes.

45 CFR 92.210 places an ongoing duty on covered entities to make reasonable efforts to identify tools that use race, color, national origin, sex, age, or disability as inputs. Utah HB 452 requires mental health chatbots to implement measures against discriminatory treatment. Compliance is therefore required regardless of the evidence gap, though "reasonable efforts" remains undefined by outcome data.

No supplied study measures algorithmic discrimination or its mitigation in any population, including Medicaid enrollees, safety-net patients, people with limited English proficiency, or people with low literacy. The groups the regulation aims to protect therefore have no evidence showing which inventory or audit methods reduce unequal treatment for them.

No supplied study documents how often protected-characteristic inputs produce harmful decisions or how severe those harms are. Without hazard data, a health system cannot estimate how many errors an inventory would catch before they reach patients. The radiology multi-society statement acknowledges that no straightforward process exists for identifying these biases.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare health systems or units that conduct structured inventories and bias audits of decision support tools with those that do not, measuring the number of discriminatory tools detected, the changes made, and subsequent differences in care decisions and outcomes across race, sex, age, disability, and national origin groups. Studies should also report the staff time and cost of meeting the reasonable-efforts standard.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems serving these groups have no direct evidence on which identification and mitigation methods work for them and may need to collect their own subgroup performance data during use.
